# 26. Translations — Concept, Review Guide and Catalogue

> **v4.7 (2026-10-24).** This file is the one place for everything about the translations of the web application: how they are organised, how a native speaker checks them, how the status code manuals reach every designated language, and — in section 9, generated from the code — every translation the application contains. Scope of what is translated at all: [10-ui-ux-specification.md](10-ui-ux-specification.md) §10a. The requirements are FR-161, FR-164, FR-166 and FR-167 ([03-srs.md](03-srs.md) §1.17); the generator is `scripts/gen_translations_doc.py`.

## 1. Purpose and what is in this file

Nineteen languages are offered (English is the source). All nineteen are complete since v4.9 (FR-167); the 18 besides English were written as proposals by the maintainer's tooling and none of them has been checked by a native speaker yet. Nobody who builds the tool can judge whether a Georgian or Odia sentence is right, so the translations have to be **checkable by a native speaker without knowing anything about the software**. The review is therefore done **in the application itself**, in its own section *Translations* (screens S42 to S44): the reviewer sees one row per string with its context and answers in one word, an Administrator or StCd Owner decides on the proposals, and an accepted proposal is shown at once. The review is recorded and tied to the exact version that was reviewed. A spreadsheet is available for reviewers who prefer to work offline.

| Part | Where it lives | Who changes it |
|---|---|---|
| Concept and review guide | sections 1–8 of this file (hand-written) | the maintainer |
| The catalogue of all translations | section 9 of this file (**generated**, do not edit by hand) | `python scripts/gen_translations_doc.py --write` |
| The review (assignments, answers, proposals, decisions) | the application, section *Translations*; tables `language_reviewer`, `translation_review`, `translation_review_item`, `translation_override` | the reviewers and the Administrator or StCd Owner |
| One review sheet per language | XLSX, downloaded in the review screen or generated with the script (section 3.2); the offline way, uploaded again | nobody, it is an output |
| The shipped translations | `app/i18n_de.py`, `app/i18n_extra.py`, `app/i18n_ar.py`, `app/i18n_in.py`, `app/i18n_eu.py` | the maintainer; accepted overrides are moved in here at a release (section 3.4) |

## 2. The four layers of translated text

A translation is not one thing. Four kinds of text are translated in different ways and are checked in different ways.

| Layer | What it is | Source of truth | Languages today | Checked by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Interface text** | navigation, buttons, labels, hints, role names | the catalogues (section 9) | 19 (all complete since v4.9; none checked by a native speaker yet) | a native speaker, with the sheet of section 3 |
| **B. Status code content** | title, description and remedy text of every status code revision | the database, `revision_translation` (FR-110) | any active language of the language lookup; German seeded | a native speaker who knows the domain, with approval by a second person (BR-018) |
| **C. Manual and export text** | the words around the content of an exported manual: column headings, title page, footers, banners | the exporters, read through the catalogues since v4.9.2 (section 5) | all languages (title page, PDF headings, footer, banner) | a native speaker, with the same sheet as layer A once the text is in a catalogue |
| **D. Help and documentation** | the in-application help, the user manual | help texts in the code; `23-user-manual.md` | help in German; manual in English | a native speaker, only after A to C |

What is **never** translated — identifiers, numbers, stored codes such as `DRAFT` or `ERROR`, audit entries, API field names, names of people — is fixed in [10-ui-ux-specification.md](10-ui-ux-specification.md) §10a and applies to all four layers.

## 3. The concept: how a native speaker checks a language

### 3.1 Principles

1. **One row, one decision.** Every string has a stable id (`S` plus six characters, derived from the English text, so it survives re-ordering), the screens that show it, the English source and the current translation. The reviewer answers per row.
2. **Context is part of the row.** The *Screens* column names the pages that use the string, so a one-word button is not translated in a vacuum.
3. **The reviewer needs no tools.** A browser and an account are enough (an external native speaker gets a Viewer account that sees only this section); the same rows are also in this file and in an ordinary spreadsheet for anybody who prefers to read or to work offline.
4. **Answers are three words.** `OK`, `CHANGE` (with a proposal) or `UNCLEAR` (with a comment). Everything else is free text.
5. **A review is tied to a version.** The review stores the fingerprint of the text the reviewer saw; the overview shows when later changes make a review out of date.
6. **Missing is as visible as wrong.** A second view lists every string that still has no translation, so a reviewer can fill gaps in the same sitting.
7. **Nobody decides on their own proposal.** The reviewer proposes, an Administrator or StCd Owner decides, and a decision is final (the same segregation as BR-018 for status code translations).

### 3.2 The reviewer's kit

| Item | How to get it |
|---|---|
| The review screen (S43) | sidebar *Translations* → the language → *Check translations* (rows with a translation) or *Missing translations*; filter by screen, search text or answer; 40 rows per page; *Mark the rest of this page OK* |
| The language's section in this file | section 9, one table per language, grouped by screen |
| The review sheet (XLSX) of one language | *Download the sheet* in the review screen, or `python scripts/gen_translations_doc.py --xlsx ar -o out/` (or `--xlsx all`); tabs **Review** (current translations, verdict list, proposal and comment columns), **Missing** (strings without translation) and **Checklist**; the completed sheet is uploaded in the same screen |
| Right-to-left languages | Arabic and Urdu are shown and set up right to left in the translation and proposal cells, in the screen and in the sheet |
| A look at the real screens | the application in the language to check (language menu, top bar) |

### 3.3 The checklist

The reviewer looks at every row for these seven things (the same list is in *What to check* of the review screen and on the third tab of each sheet).

| Check | The question |
|---|---|
| Meaning | Does the translation say what the English says, no more and no less? |
| Terminology | Are the fixed terms the same everywhere (Status Code, Draft, Release, Reviewer)? Terms that stay in English are in section 4.3. |
| Fit | Is it short enough for a button, a column heading or a menu entry? |
| Register | Is the form of address right for a technical tool: formal, neutral, no slang? |
| Placeholders | Are markers such as `%(n)s` kept exactly, in a sensible place? |
| Script and direction | Right script; digits and identifiers left in Latin; correct right to left? |
| Spelling and punctuation | Spelling, accents, quotation marks, final full stop. |

### 3.4 From assignment to a shown translation

1. An **Administrator or StCd Owner assigns** one or more reviewers to the language (*Translations* → *Decisions and reviewers*). Any active account can be assigned; the assignment is audited (`LANGUAGE_REVIEWER_ASSIGN`, `LANGUAGE_REVIEWER_REMOVE`).
2. The reviewer opens *Translations*, which lists only the languages they are assigned to, and works through the rows: **OK**, **CHANGE** with a proposal, or **UNCLEAR** with a comment. Answers are saved page by page and can be continued any time; a sheet filled in offline is uploaded and read into the same answers.
3. The reviewer **completes the review** when every translated string has a verdict. The completion is recorded with the date and the fingerprint of the version the review was started on (`TRANSLATION_REVIEW_COMPLETE`).  Proposals for missing translations are possible on the way but are not a condition for completing it.
4. An Administrator or StCd Owner who is **not** the proposer opens *Decisions and reviewers* and **accepts** (optionally correcting the text), **rejects** or **notes** each open item (`TRANSLATION_PROPOSAL_DECIDE`). Only a proposed change can be accepted; an UNCLEAR item is noted or dismissed. A decision is final.
5. An accepted change becomes an **override** and is **shown at once** in the application, for that language only, with no release and no restart. An override can be removed again, which brings the shipped text back (`TRANSLATION_OVERRIDE_REMOVE`).
6. At the next release the maintainer moves the overrides into the catalogue file of the language and regenerates this file; the override then equals the shipped text and is removed.
7. The next visit of an assigned reviewer starts a new review. **A follow-up review covers only what is new or changed since the last approval** (*New and changed translations*; *All translations* shows the rest); what was approved stays approved. Approved means: an OK answer, an accepted proposal (its final text), a rejected proposal or a noted question; an undecided proposal approves nothing. Section 3.5 tells the state of the language.

### 3.5 Review states

The overview (S42) shows one state per language.

| State | Meaning | What it should mean for use (recommended, section 8) |
|---|---|---|
| not reviewed | nobody who speaks the language has completed a review of it | the language is marked as a beta in the language menu; not offered to customers |
| in progress | a review is open | as above |
| reviewed | a native speaker completed a review and no string awaits approval | offered without marking |
| changed since the review | strings are new or were changed after they were approved (a shipped change, an override) | stays offered; the language keeps the *beta* mark for the working roles, a Viewer reads those strings in English until they are approved, and a **follow-up review** lists only them (FR-176) |

### 3.6 Who reviews

A native speaker of the language who has used the product or knows its field (controller software, wind turbines). Two people are required where a mistake could mislead an operator: layer B (status code content) always, layer A only for the strings that appear in warnings and confirmations. For the Indian languages one reviewer per language is needed even where languages seem close (Hindi and Marathi share a script, not their wording).

### 3.7 When

Before a language is shown to anybody who relies on it, and then at every release for the strings that changed since the last review. Because the review stores the fingerprint of a whole language, a change is detected for the language, and a follow-up review is a new review of the whole language (section 8, item 5).

## 4. Status code manuals in all designated languages

### 4.1 What "designated" means

The *designated languages* are the active entries of the language lookup (`lookup_language`, Administration → Lookups): today the nineteen languages of section 9. Deactivating a language in the lookup removes it from the translation screens and the export options; it does not delete translations. English is the source of every status code.

### 4.2 What exists today

| Step | Today |
|---|---|
| A translation of title, description and remedy text per language | `revision_translation` with the states MISSING, DRAFT, APPROVED (FR-110); saved only against an Approved or Released revision; approved by a Reviewer or Administrator who is not the translator (BR-018) |
| Carry-over to the next revision | as DRAFT, on request |
| Worklist | the codes still without an approved translation in a language (FR-111) |
| An export in a language | CSV, JSON, XLSX and PDF of a Release or of all Released codes, in the language, using approved translations only; a code without one shows the English text and is marked (`content_language`), or the export is *strict* and refuses (FR-111) |
| Audience, profile, software version | independent of the language (FR-100 … FR-107) |

### 4.3 Terminology shared by the interface and the content

A manual is only trustworthy if the same term is used in the interface, in the status code texts and in the manual. One list per language, kept next to the catalogue and handed to every reviewer, fixes the terms. The first column says what is **never** translated.

| Term | Rule |
|---|---|
| `StCd`, `StCd-01000`, `PrgIdx_GUi`, `2XM` / `3XM` / `4XM`, `MC`, `HC`, group and subgroup codes (`010xx`, `1110x`) | never translated; Latin letters and digits in every language |
| Status Code, Draft, Review, Approved, Released, Deprecated, Archived | one fixed translation per language, used in the interface and in the manual headings; the English code stays in data and exports |
| Main Controller, Hub Controller | the descriptive name is translated per language (German: Hauptsteuerung, Nabensteuerung); the abbreviations `MC` and `HC` stay |
| Alarm, Set delay, Reset delay, Snapshot, Availability group | one fixed translation per language; the first time a manual uses the term the English word may follow in brackets |
| Product and standard names, units (`ms`, `s`, `min`) | never translated |

**Built in v4.9 (FR-166):** the list is the section *Terminology* of the application (S45 to S47, section 8a) with 78 terms in seven categories and a draft translation in every language, kept apart from the interface translations.

### 4.4 What is missing for "every manual in every language"

| Gap | Concept |
|---|---|
| **Coverage is only visible per language, not per release.** | A matrix *codes × languages* for a Release (counts and percentages) on the Release page and in the export manifest, and a readiness rule: a language is **ready** for a Release when every Released code in it has an APPROVED translation. A manual in a language that is not ready is still possible but carries a visible banner and the per-row marker of FR-111. |
| **Anybody with the role Reviewer may approve a translation, whatever the language.** In nineteen languages nobody can judge them all. | Language competence on the user (*can approve Georgian*, …). A translation is approved only by a user with that competence who is not the translator (BR-018 extended). Without competence a user can still translate and see the worklist. |
| **Translating hundreds of codes one by one in a form does not scale.** | The same round trip as for the interface (section 3): export a *content sheet* per language (identifier, English title, description, remedy text, empty target columns, only codes without approved translation), the translator fills it, the import stores every row as a DRAFT translation, approval stays a separate step. Machine suggestions may fill the sheet but are marked and never approved automatically. |
| **One export per language is a manual job.** | *Export all languages*: one request builds one file per ready language and a manifest of the coverage, as a ZIP, with the same SHA-256 manifest as a single export (FR-103). |
| ~~The words around the content are English~~ **solved in v4.9.2 (FR-171)** for the PDF and its title page; the headings of CSV, JSON and XLSX stay the field names by design. | The text is in the catalogues and in the review sheets like layer A; a manual in a language prints its own words. |
| **The PDF cannot print Hindi, Arabic, Georgian, Bengali and the other scripts.** *Solved in v4.7 (FR-165, I-37).* | A Noto font per script with HarfBuzz shaping (Devanagari for Hindi and Marathi, Bengali, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Kannada, Odia, Malayalam, Gurmukhi for Punjabi, Naskh Arabic, Nastaliq Urdu, Georgian) and right-to-left layout for Arabic and Urdu, bundled with the application (`app/static/fonts/`). The PDF is therefore offered for every language. |
| **Nobody checks the finished manual.** | A *spot-check sample* per language: the first twenty codes of the Release exported in the language, with the interface text and the manual text, handed to the reviewer of that language together with the sheet. |

### 4.5 The check of a manual in one language

1. The Release is published; the coverage matrix shows the language as ready (or the banner says what is missing).
2. The manual is exported in the language (CSV, JSON, XLSX, DOCX and, since v4.7, PDF in every script).
3. The reviewer of the language reads the spot-check sample against the English original: title and description make sense to an operator, the fixed terms of section 4.3 are used, units and identifiers are untouched.
4. The result is noted on the Release (reviewer, date, language); the export manifest carries the language and its coverage.

| Administrator, StCd Owner | assign the reviewers of each language and decide on their proposals (never on their own) |

| StCd Owner | decides which languages are *designated* (active) and when a language leaves beta |

## 8a. The technical nomenclature (v4.9)

The interface translations (layer A) and the words of the product are different things. *Status Code*, *Hub Controller*, *Set delay* or *Draft* must read the same in the interface, in the status code texts and in the manual, and the person who chooses the word has to know the controller, not only the language. The tool therefore keeps these words in a vocabulary of its own, the section *Terminology* (S45 to S47, FR-166), apart from the review of the interface strings.

| Aspect | How it is built |
|---|---|
| Terms | 78 terms ship with the tool in seven categories — 21 product words, 8 data words, 9 states, 18 process words, 6 roles, 9 audiences and 7 that are never translated (`StCd`, `MC`, `HC` and similar); each has a code that never changes, the English text and a meaning for a translator who does not know the product |
| Translations | one per term and language, 18 languages; the shipped ones are **drafts**, taken from the interface catalogue where both contain the word |
| Approval | a translation is a draft until **a second person** approves it (the segregation of BR-018); *Send back* needs a note and reopens an approved translation; a changed English text reopens every approval of the term |
| Who | everybody signed in reads; Engineer, Reviewer, Administrator, StCd Owner and Chief Engineer propose; Reviewer, Administrator, StCd Owner and Chief Engineer approve; Administrator, StCd Owner and Chief Engineer add and change terms; the reviewer of an interface language has no right here |
| Check | S47 lists the interface strings that contain a term whose translation is missing from the translation of the string; it is a hint, because languages that inflect words change the ending |
| Export | XLSX and CSV per language and for all languages (a formula in a cell is neutralised); a translation office can work offline |
| Audit | `TERM_CREATE`, `TERM_UPDATE`, `TERM_TRANSLATE`, `TERM_APPROVE`, `TERM_REJECT` (AUD-077) |

What it does not do yet: the terms are not substituted into the interface automatically — the interface catalogues are written once and the consistency check shows where they differ from the approved vocabulary — and the status code manuals do not read the vocabulary (section 4.4).

## 8b. Critical review of the language implementation (v4.9)

The implementation of v4.5 to v4.8 was reviewed for what a person who opens the application in Hindi or Arabic actually sees. The findings and what was done about each:

| # | Finding | What was done |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The administration pages (export profiles, integrations, lookups, backups, review checklist, stalled requests, user management) and several other templates carried English literals that no `_()` wrapped, so a translated interface switched back to English there | all of them are wrapped; the inventory is read from the templates, so a new literal without `_()` is found by `test_every_template_string_has_a_german_entry` |
| 2 | Flash messages and the reasons a service gives for a refusal were English | the screens translate what they flash (`flash(_(…))`), and `app/i18n_messages.py` finds the sentences by reading the source (`raise …Error("…")`), so the inventory cannot miss one; a field name passed to an error is not a sentence and is left out |
| 3 | The content security policy allows fonts from the application only, and the fonts a browser falls back on do not draw every script reliably | the Noto fonts are served from `/static/fonts` through `@font-face` rules with `unicode-range`, so a page that does not use a script never downloads its font |
| 4 | Long translations (Malayalam, Tamil, Odia, German) stretched tables and pushed the page wider than the window | `.table-scroll` around wide tables and `min-width: 0` on the main column |
| 5 | Placeholders (`%(n)s`) could be damaged by a translation | a test compares the placeholders of every catalogue entry with its English source, for all languages |
| 6 | Completeness was tested for German only | the same test now covers the 18 other languages (`test_every_language_translates_the_whole_interface_inventory`) and the document of section 9 is generated from the same catalogues |
| 7 | The technical words had no home: a term could differ between the interface and a manual | the Terminology section of 8a, with a check against the interface |

What remains: (a) **no translation but the shipped ones is reviewed by a native speaker** — the 18 languages are proposals, and the review of FR-164 is the way to correct them; (b) the messages of the API, the content of the exports outside the catalogue (section 5) and the user manual are English; (c) the web interface sets Urdu in Naskh, not in the Nastaliq of the PDF; (d) the terms of the Terminology section are not yet applied to the interface automatically.

## 8c. The confidence check (v4.10)

Before a native speaker has looked at a language, a **pre-check** says how far its text can be trusted. It is done by an AI checker (Claude) and is **not a review**: it does not remove the *beta* mark, it approves nothing, and it is no substitute for the native speakers of section 3. It tells the reviewers where to look first and the business how much work to expect.

**Method.**

1. *Every string, mechanically.* Placeholders kept, nothing missing, no untranslated English where a translation is expected, and every term of the nomenclature (section 8a) rendered as the nomenclature says when it stands alone.
2. *A sample, read.* The same 160 strings in every language (60 short, 100 longer, drawn with a fixed seed from the 1,190) are read for meaning, register, consistency and the form of the technical terms. A **wrong meaning** counts 1, an **awkward or inconsistent wording** 0.5.
3. *From the sample to a percentage.* The rate of the sample is carried over to the whole catalogue; from it are taken the **haircut** - what the checker cannot see in that language (4 points for German, French, Spanish and Italian, which it reads fluently, up to 16 for Odia, where it can judge only the surface) - and half a finding for every term that the interface renders differently from the nomenclature. The result is the estimated share of strings a native speaker would accept unchanged.
4. *The colour.* The overview of the application (Translations) and the table 9.1 show the percentage on a colour in steps of five points: **red at 50 % or less, yellow around 75 %, green above 95 %**.

**Result of 2026-10-24** (table 9.1 and 9.1a): the Latin-script languages come out between 92 % and 95 %, the languages of India, Arabic, Urdu and Georgian between 83 % and 88 %, Odia at 78 %. No language is above 95 %, so none is green: the checker would not put its name to that, and the haircut says so. The findings that stand out are the same in several languages and are worth settling once: *escalation* (the separate escalation code pool) was rendered as appeal, increase, intensity or *additional* in Tamil, Odia, Hindi, Marathi, Urdu, Kannada, Malayalam and Punjabi; *attributable* (what a deleted user did stays attributable) as *accusable* in Kannada and Malayalam; *revision* and *review* are the same word in Arabic and *revision* is *version* in Odia; *released* is *free* in Odia; and the *signing secret* is rendered literally in many languages. Odia also has an invented word for *deployment*. The flagged strings are listed in table 9.1a; **they have not been corrected**, because a correction by the same checker would be as unverified as the text; the native speaker decides.

**The terms.** Between 2 and 18 strings per language (136 in all) that stand for a term of the nomenclature are rendered differently from it (for example *Main controller* and *Hub controller* in the languages of India, *Release* in Odia). Some of these are legitimate - a plural or an inflected form - and the check counts them as half a finding each. Which of the two is right is for the reviewers and for the owner of the nomenclature; until they decide, the interface and the glossary stay as they are.

**Every change goes through the check.** A string that is added or changed, and any change of a term of the nomenclature, has to be read one by one and recorded:

```bash
python scripts/translation_precheck.py --check                  # what changed since the last check
python scripts/translation_precheck.py --template > delta.json  # one line per changed string
python scripts/translation_precheck.py --delta delta.json       # verdict OK, A (awkward) or E (wrong) for each
```

The record (`app/translations/precheck.json`) keeps the percentage of every language, the findings and who recorded what; `precheck_state.json` holds a short hash of every string at the last check. `--delta` refuses a changed string without a verdict and a changed nomenclature without the confirmation that the interface was compared with it, and `test_every_change_of_the_text_or_the_nomenclature_has_been_through_the_check` fails as long as the record is out of date, so a change cannot be released unchecked. The percentage of a language is recomputed from the sample rate for the strings that did not change and from the verdicts for those that did. A new full pre-check (`--baseline scripts/precheck_baseline.json`) is due when the share of strings read one by one has grown large, or when a language has been reviewed and its errors are known.

**The StCd Owner is told (FR-178).** Two things report what a change of the vocabulary does to the languages, in the notices of the application (kind `TRANSLATION_IMPACT`):

| When | What the notice says | Who gets it |
|---|---|---|
| A version is deployed or the server starts, and the shipped text or nomenclature differs from the last confidence check (`flask translation-impact` does the same by hand; the installers run it after the database upgrade) | the changed strings per language, whether the nomenclature changed, the reviewed languages with strings awaiting approval; the reminder to record the confidence check | the StCd Owners and the reviewers assigned to an affected language |
| A term is **added** or **changed** in *Terminology*, or the translation of a term is **approved** | the languages without an approved translation, the interface strings that do not use the term (counted per language), the reviewed languages whose strings need a follow-up review; for an approval the one language | the StCd Owners and the reviewers assigned to an affected language |

A notice is sent once per change and person; a failing notice never undoes the change. The test of this section runs in the build and covers what ships; the notice covers what is changed while the application runs and what a deployment brings.

**And the approval of the native speakers is separate.** New and changed strings are approved by a follow-up review, not by the confidence check (FR-176, section 3.4).
